fields.statement: Genesis keeps the model of a product, what it is, why it is that way and what is planned, inside its repo, so anyone can build quality software with agents.
Genesis describes a product as one model: a fixed set of node kinds, typed links between them, one tree of capabilities, with IDs and handles.
Genesis changes the model through change sets that are created, revised, proposed, accepted or rejected, landed, and rebased when they conflict.
Genesis remembers why: it walks back from any node to the decisions, change sets, sources and actors that shaped it.
Genesis reads the model back in the shape each reader needs: a node, the tree, lists, a slice for a task, the roadmap and what is ready, as it is, will be or would be.
Genesis keeps the model true: it checks the log and its links, renders it as markdown, and finds where the model and the code drift apart.
Genesis teaches agents to use it: the guide in the binary, the skills, installing them, a session-start brief, and evals.
Anyone can build quality software with agents, using as little or as much of Genesis as they want.
The model tells the truth about what the product is and why.
Agents get small, accurate context.
Power users and agents first; everyone else later.
The log is append-only, and only the CLI writes it.
The same model always gives the same bytes.
Nothing outside an adapter names an agent.
Our state never lives in Rex.
Rex is required from the runtime up.
No prompts without a terminal.
Bypassed permissions only on a dedicated machine.
